MiniLAW: Ministry of Law is a bold and energetic indie action game that blends retro sensibilities with dystopian cyberpunk themes, offering an experience that feels both nostalgic and inventive. Developed and published by Lasso Games, the title places players in the role of a cybernetically enhanced law enforcer known as the Constable, tasked with maintaining order in the sprawling megacity of New Babel. From the start, the game establishes a world defined by excess, corruption, and perpetual crisis, drawing clear inspiration from classic science-fiction law enforcement stories while carving out its own identity through gameplay systems and tone.

The setting of New Babel functions as more than a backdrop; it is the central engine that drives the experience. Crime is rampant and ever-present, and the city is divided into districts where different threats emerge dynamically. Rather than following a rigid mission structure, players are encouraged to patrol, respond to incidents, and decide how to confront unfolding situations. This open-ended approach gives the game a sense of unpredictability, as crimes can escalate or resolve depending on player intervention, reinforcing the fantasy of being an ever-watchful agent of the Ministry of Law rather than a scripted hero moving from level to level.

Combat is fast-paced and multifaceted, combining side-scrolling shooter mechanics with platforming and tactical decision-making. The Constable’s enhanced abilities allow for powerful jumps, heavy strikes, and efficient gunplay, but success depends on positioning, timing, and awareness rather than raw firepower alone. Enemies come in many forms, from street gangs and armed criminals to more heavily armored or mutated foes, each requiring different approaches. The game encourages experimentation by offering both lethal and non-lethal options, rewarding players who arrest suspects and maintain order with greater efficiency rather than simply eliminating every threat.

Progression in MiniLAW is handled through a flexible upgrade system that allows players to tailor their Constable to their preferred playstyle. Completing missions and responding to crimes earns resources that can be invested in improved weapons, defensive upgrades, and specialized modules that enhance mobility or crowd control. This progression system adds a strategic layer to the action, as players must decide which upgrades best suit their approach to policing the city. Over time, these enhancements significantly change how encounters play out, making the sense of growth tangible and satisfying.

Visually, the game embraces a detailed pixel art style that captures the grit and vibrancy of its cyberpunk world. Neon-lit streets, towering structures, and chaotic urban environments create a strong sense of place, while character animations and effects convey impact and momentum during combat. The presentation balances clarity with flair, ensuring that the fast-paced action remains readable even during intense encounters. Complementing the visuals is a soundtrack infused with electronic and industrial influences, reinforcing the game’s high-energy tone and dystopian atmosphere.

The difficulty curve in MiniLAW can be demanding, particularly for players unfamiliar with its mechanics. Early encounters may feel overwhelming as the game offers limited guidance, requiring players to learn through experimentation and failure. Controls can feel stiff at first, but with time they reveal a depth that supports precise movement and combat once mastered. This steep learning curve may deter some players, but for others it becomes a key part of the game’s appeal, making each successful encounter feel earned.

Overall, MiniLAW: Ministry of Law is a distinctive and ambitious indie title that thrives on its combination of emergent gameplay, retro action, and cyberpunk worldbuilding. While it may show some rough edges in pacing and accessibility, its core systems are engaging and rewarding, especially for players who enjoy challenging action games with room for creativity and personal expression. By blending law enforcement fantasy with tactical choice and fast-paced combat, MiniLAW delivers an experience that stands out in the indie space as both a homage to classic influences and a confident statement of its own design vision.

An exceptionally satisfying process of beating and gunning down innumerable citizens of dubious moral character to slowly gather intel on the location of THE BOMB.

Undeniably buggy but not game-breakingly so.

Hard to learn, but once you've got the hang of being a grossly overpowered Dredd-like in a suit of power-armour they can barely control, it becomes *disturbingly* satisfying to blast your way at speed through ragged towerblocks full of heavily armed mercenary thugs and club-wielding mutants. 

It's a remarkably cleverly designed fusion of horrible power fantasy and tactical side-scrolling shooter. You won't struggle to win a given battle once you've got some good upgrades, but you'll struggle to optimise your income of requisition points for good conduct if you don't take perps alive, and ideally surrendering while conscious.

The use of health, endurance and morale as three different resources is great - being able to intimidate suspects by shouting them down, firing near them and injuring them, while trying not to kill them, and accepting battered unconsciousness as an acceptable middle-ground is remarkably well-balanced and never wholly predictable, even when you're firing 13mm magnum rounds through three people and one of them survives a cripple to beg you not to finish them off.

The game has remarkably fluidity and depth to the combat and movement systems, for what feels initially like a clunky and overly complex game. Once it clicks, it feels great to move around and fight.

And alongside that you've got the narrative side of the game, using a 12-key 80s-90s style videophone to request advice and support, investigate a few minor leads, and perform remote interrogations of captured suspects and voluntary informants while guiding the broad strokes of your department's investigatory campaign.

Ultimately a very repetitive game, but very intentionally so - as the time to detonation ticks down, you'll be desperately taking down perps at robberies, hostage situations and assault sites trying to find any clue as to which of the hidden HQs contains the bomb or the code to disarm it. Surprisingly tense, and having beaten it on my third try (albeit with a less than perfect ending), I'll definitely come back again one day when this suits the right mood.

Donc, des fois, prendre le risque de se faire descendre pour pouvoir arrêter les criminels plutôt que de les tuer d'un coup, ça sera plus rentable et rendra d'autres descentes plus simples du fait d'une meilleure préparation. 
En ce qui concerne l'enquête : il y a quatre Gang, et chaque gang à trois industries d'activités (trafic de drogue ; trafic d'armes, etc...) Chaque trafic à un QG, et donc, chaque gang a trois QG.
[Alors, je suis déjà tomber (en mode normal) sur un Gang qui avait 4 secteur d'activités, je sais pas : peut-être la difficulté.]
 
Pour les niveaux, on se déplace en voiture sur la map de Neo Babel, en se rendant sur les lieux d'un crime ou d'un QG.
Les déplacements coûtent du temps. Ce qui pourrait vous faire échouer une partie car vous n'aurez pas su gérer vos temps de déplacement. Petit truc sympa : dans les aptitudes améliorables de vôtre perso, il y a CONDUITE, qui permet de se déplacer plus vite dans la ville, et économiser du temps que vous pourrez consacrer à vous concentrer sur le terrain, et pas vous dépêcher pour économiser du temps.
Attention pour les QG : si vous attaquez un QG, et que la bombe n'y est pas, les emplacements de TOUS les QG du gang attaqué se déplaceront, et vous ne saurez plus rien d'eux.
On enquêtera surplace en trouvant des indices sur les criminels. Ou bien, en passant des coups de fils ! Et bien gérer ses appels permet d'avoir plus d'infos, et de retrouver plus vite la bombe (ou de la retrouver tout court).

   Un jeu qui a le bon goût de diversifier son gameplay : de l'action, de la stratégie (aussi pour gérer son temps pour retrouver la bombe), de l'enquête avec un petit système de choix dans les dialogues.

Dernière précision : ce jeu génère (à priori) une génération aléatoire des secteurs d'activité des gangs. et aussi des ennemis présent dans chaque niveau.

Bref c'est cool, un rogue-lite qui a de quoi vous faire passer du bon temps.

[h1]I guess the best way to put it is that I like everything about this game except actually playing it.[/h1]

I bought this game years ago. Probably the week it released into EA on Steam. It's basically a Judge Dredd game with enough changed to avoid a lawsuit. I'm fine with that though. I love Dredd and 2000AD and when I saw this game I bought it immediately despite it being early in EA. 

Booting it up though presented you with a barebones mess of a game. Not much to it and controller support was literally only partial. I didn't like it so it just languished in my library until a week or two ago when I thought of it again. I saw that it had come out of EA, and as it's been years since I touched it I redownloaded the game.

I'm almost positive the intro animatic and some of the RPG elements had been added since I played. The only thing I really remembered from years ago was selecting the location on the map, flying there and playing the level. Pretty much nothing else. So the additions impressed me. Also, controllers fully work now so that's good.

But what hadn't changed were the controls. Meaning, your guy is stiff and controls awkwardly... until you press up and he starts bouncing quickly and all over the place. Up (or W) being jump doesn't help. The missions seem slightly repetitive as well, but I only got through a handful before the controls started to get to me again. 

So:

Is this game pretty to look at?: Yes
Does it have a great soundtrack?: Yes
Does it ooze style?: Yes
Do you play as Judge Dredd?: Pretty much
Do you play as Sylvester Stallone's Judge Dredd?: Thank god no
Are the controls well done and fluid?: No
Do the controls frustrate: Yes, and quickly
Do the levels seem repetitive?: A bit

Although the launch out of Early Access had some bumps, I enjoyed this game enough to keep restarting it when it crashed to desktop on me. The devs have been quick to respond to bug reports and suggestions on the forums, so now that they've fixed those crashes, I can't see a reason not to recommend it. 

Some important things to know when starting out though:
- The default keyboard controls are baffling, use the tutorial to learn what everything does, then bind them to buttons you can easily use.

- Controllers are great for pick up and play, but rebind secondary weapon if you want to use grenades. If you stick to melee weapons everything works from the start

- Spend at least a bit on the driving skill if your starting background doesn't include it, unless you're on easy. You will have to try to run out of time on easy.

If you've played the Dredd vs Death first person shooter, it reminds me of that; you can just kill every criminal in sight, but the game rewards you for capturing them alive. I find the priority targets a nice middle ground compared to the Dredd game as well. You can focus on capturing these targets alive for their higher reward, then start guns blazing once you know they won't get caught in the crossfire. There is a nuclear bomb to stop after all!

[b]A short but sweet ride, if you prepare for some (rapidly vanishing) rough edges[/b]

When I first bought this game for launch.  Optional tutorial phone calls would crash the game, and I swiftly was soft locked by being trapped inside a wall.  The devs fixed the latter that night, and the former (along with a bunch of phone issues) with their recent overhaul patch.

A beautiful game to start the new year with! Lemme try and do a pro/con brekadown...

PROS
-Great art and animations
-Music that greatly enhances the encounters
-A story that gives you a limited amount of time, giving you a sense of urgency and dread as the time ticks down
-Gives a sense of great power and strength, but at the same time you feel quite vulnerable
-PUNCH CRIME. YELL AT CRIME.
-The ability to nonlethally take down perps, even if you may have to pop a round or two in them

CONS
-Controls are somewhat clunky, often found myself hitting the wrong button in times of stress
-The UI is overwhelming at first, but something you get used to
-YOU CAN SKIP CUTSCENES, BE CAREFUL! 
-Relatively short. I beat a Normal run in about 5 hours, but there is stuff to encourage multiple playthroughs
-Side stories in the main game feel like they compete with your attention, making it hard to try and finish them and not explode violently
-Occasional extreme lag, making some areas move in slow motion. Unsure the cause.

There's probably more, but for a game that just recently emerged from early access, they've done a damn good job. If you like a mix of Cyberpunk 2020, Robocop, and Judge Dredd you'll probably enjoy this.
